---
title: "Graphs, Networks, and Knowledge-Graph Embeddings"
---

Much biological knowledge is relational. Proteins interact with proteins, genes
regulate genes, enzymes catalyse reactions in pathways, and drugs act on targets
that are implicated in diseases. A single entity is rarely informative in
isolation; its role emerges from its neighbors. This chapter treats relational
data as a graph, defines embeddings of its nodes and edges, and distinguishes
three prediction tasks that are easy to confuse: node-level prediction,
edge-level (link) prediction, and knowledge-graph completion. It then moves from
shallow random-walk embeddings to graph neural networks and multi-relational
knowledge-graph embeddings, and closes with applications in drug repurposing,
target identification, and function prediction.

Following Appendix A, vectors are bold lowercase ($\mathbf{z}$, $\mathbf{e}$),
matrices are bold uppercase ($\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{W}$), and
scalars are italic. A graph has $n=|V|$ nodes; node embeddings at layer $l$ are
$\mathbf{z}_v^{(l)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_l}$ and are stacked row-wise into
$\mathbf{Z}^{(l)} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_l}$; a knowledge-graph fact
$(h,r,t)$ has head, relation, and tail embeddings
$\mathbf{e}_h, \mathbf{e}_r, \mathbf{e}_t \in \mathbb{R}^k$ (or $\mathbb{C}^k$ for
the complex models); $\sigma$ is the logistic sigmoid and $\odot$ the Hadamard
product.

# Biological Graphs and Their Properties

::: {.callout-note}
## Definition
**Graph.** A graph $G = (V, E)$ consists of a set of nodes $V$ and a set of edges
$E \subseteq V \times V$. In a *typed* or *heterogeneous* graph each node and edge
carries a type; a knowledge-graph fact is a triple $(h, r, t)$ with a head entity
$h$, relation $r$, and tail entity $t$, and such triples are the atomic facts of a
knowledge graph.
:::

Biological graphs differ along four axes: what the nodes are, whether edges are
directed, whether edges are weighted or signed, and whether the graph is
homogeneous or typed.

| Graph | Nodes | Edges | Typical source |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Protein--protein interaction | Proteins | Physical or functional association, weighted by confidence | STRING [@szklarczyk2019string] |
| Gene regulatory | Genes / transcription factors | Directed regulatory influence | Reconstructed from expression and binding data |
| Metabolic | Metabolites | Enzyme-catalysed reactions | KEGG pathways [@kanehisa2000kegg] |
| Gene--disease | Genes and diseases | Undirected associations | DisGeNET [@pinero2020disgenet] |
| Biomedical knowledge graph | Drugs, genes, diseases, pathways | Typed relations | Hetionet [@himmelstein2017systematic] |

Several properties shape algorithm choice. Interaction graphs are noisy and
incomplete, so the goal is often to denoise or complete them rather than classify
existing edges. Regulatory graphs are directed and asymmetric, so a
neighborhood-aggregation scheme that ignores direction loses information.
Gene--disease and drug--gene graphs are heterogeneous, so a single relation type
cannot represent them. These graphs also tend to be sparse and heavy-tailed, with
a few high-degree hubs and many low-degree nodes, which biases random-walk and
message-passing methods toward hubs unless corrected.

# Shallow Node Embeddings

The first generation of graph embeddings reuses the shallow prediction objectives
of Chapter 3. A random walk over the graph produces sequences of nodes, and a
skip-gram model learns one vector per node from those sequences.

DeepWalk runs uniform random walks from each node and trains the SGNS objective on
the resulting (node, context) pairs [@perozzi2014deepwalk]. node2vec generalizes
the walk distribution with return and in-out parameters $p$ and $q$, controlling
whether the walk revisits its origin and whether it explores locally or
globally [@grover2016node2vec]. With node embedding $\mathbf{z}_u \in \mathbb{R}^k$
and context embedding $\mathbf{z}_c \in \mathbb{R}^k$, pair set $\mathcal{D}$
sampled from walks, $K$ negatives, and noise distribution $P_n$, the objective

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{walk}}(\{\mathbf{z}\})
= \sum_{(u,c) \in \mathcal{D}}
\Big[ \log \sigma(\mathbf{z}_u^\top \mathbf{z}_c)
+ \sum_{j=1}^{K} \mathbb{E}_{c_j \sim P_n}\!
\big( \log \sigma(-\mathbf{z}_u^\top \mathbf{z}_{c_j}) \big) \Big]
$$ {#eq-ch10-walk-sgns}

is maximized over the per-node vectors $\{\mathbf{z}_u\}$. (@eq-ch10-walk-sgns)
is exactly the SGNS objective of Chapter 3, so by the same argument it implicitly
factorizes a shifted pointwise mutual information matrix over walk co-occurrences
(Chapter 3): nodes that co-occur on many walks receive aligned vectors, which
is why the walk distribution — not the network — determines the geometry. Because
every node has a single learned vector, the embedding is *transductive*: nodes
unseen at training time have no vector, and the method cannot be applied to a new
screen without retraining. LINE instead optimizes two objectives that preserve
first-order proximity (observed edges) and second-order proximity (shared
neighborhoods) separately [@tang2015line]. Shallow embeddings are cheap and strong
on homogeneous graphs, but this transductive limitation motivates the inductive
architectures below.

# Graph Neural Networks

Graph neural networks (GNNs) learn node representations by passing messages along
edges, which makes them inductive and able to incorporate node features. The graph
neural network model is the original formulation [@scarselli2009graph]; the modern
view is the message-passing framework, in which each node updates its state from
its neighbors:

$$
\mathbf{z}_v^{(l+1)}
= \phi\!\left( \mathbf{z}_v^{(l)}, \;
\underset{u \in \mathcal{N}(v)}{\bigoplus} \;
\psi\!\left( \mathbf{z}_v^{(l)}, \mathbf{z}_u^{(l)}, \mathbf{e}_{uv} \right) \right),
$$ {#eq-ch10-mp}

where $\mathbf{z}_v^{(l)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_l}$ is the representation of node $v$
at layer $l$, $\mathcal{N}(v)$ is its neighborhood, $\mathbf{e}_{uv}$ is an
optional edge feature, $\psi$ is a (learnable) message function, $\phi$ is a
(learnable) update function, and $\bigoplus$ is a permutation-invariant
aggregation such as sum, mean, or max
[@gilmer2017neural]. (@eq-ch10-mp) is applied to every node in parallel, so
the trainable parameters are shared across nodes; a GNN stacks such layers, and
the receptive field of a node therefore grows with depth. The permutation
invariance of $\bigoplus$ is not optional — it is required so that isomorphic
neighborhoods receive the same update.

::: {.callout-note}
## Definition
**Message passing.** Message passing is an iterative scheme in which each node
computes a message from each neighbor, aggregates the messages with a
permutation-invariant operator, and combines the aggregate with its own state to
produce a new state. Two isomorphic neighborhoods must receive the same update,
which forces the aggregator to be permutation-invariant.
:::

## Layer Variants

Specific GNNs differ in how they define $\psi$, $\phi$, and the aggregator. The
graph convolutional network (GCN) arises as a first-order approximation of a
spectral graph convolution. With the symmetric normalized Laplacian
$\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{D}^{-1/2}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}^{-1/2}$ and its
eigendecomposition $\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{U}^\top$, a
spectral convolution filters a signal $\mathbf{x}$ by
$g_\theta \star \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{U}\,g_\theta(\boldsymbol{\Lambda})\,\mathbf{U}^\top \mathbf{x}$;
approximating the filter by a first-order Chebyshev polynomial in the shifted
spectrum, $g_\theta(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}) \approx \theta_0 \mathbf{I} + \theta_1 (\boldsymbol{\Lambda} - \mathbf{I})$
(eigenvalues of $\mathbf{L}$ lie in $[0,2]$, so $\lambda_{\max}=2$), gives

$$
g_\theta \star \mathbf{x}
\;\approx\; \theta_0 \mathbf{x} - \theta_1 \mathbf{D}^{-1/2}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}^{-1/2}\mathbf{x}
\;=\; \theta\left(\mathbf{I} + \mathbf{D}^{-1/2}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}^{-1/2}\right)\mathbf{x},
$$ {#eq-ch10-spectral}

where the second equality sets $\theta = \theta_0 = -\theta_1$, and a
renormalization trick replaces
$\mathbf{I} + \mathbf{D}^{-1/2}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}^{-1/2}$ by
$\tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2}\tilde{\mathbf{A}}\tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2}$ with
$\tilde{\mathbf{A}} = \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{I}$ to avoid numerical instability
[@bruna2014spectral; @defferrard2016convolutional; @kipf2017semi]. The
approximation (@eq-ch10-spectral) is local — each output depends only on a node and its
immediate neighbors — which is what makes it practical on large biological graphs.
Stacking this local filter and adding a trainable weight matrix $\mathbf{W}^{(l)}$
yields the GCN layer

$$
\mathbf{Z}^{(l+1)} = \mathrm{ReLU}\!\left(
\tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2} \tilde{\mathbf{A}} \tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2}
\mathbf{Z}^{(l)} \mathbf{W}^{(l)}
\right),
$$ {#eq-ch10-gcn}

where $\tilde{\mathbf{A}} = \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{I}$ adds self-loops,
$\tilde{D}_{ii} = \sum_j \tilde{A}_{ij}$ is its degree matrix, $\mathbf{Z}^{(l)}$
stacks node states, $\mathbf{W}^{(l)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_l \times d_{l+1}}$ is
trainable, and $\mathrm{ReLU}$ is the element-wise activation [@kipf2017semi]. Minimizing a
node-classification loss over the $\{\mathbf{W}^{(l)}\}$ then trains the layer.
GraphSAGE instead samples a fixed number of neighbors and concatenates the node
state with an aggregate of sampled neighbor states,

$$
\mathbf{z}_v^{(l+1)} = \mathrm{ReLU}\!\left(\mathbf{W}^{(l)}
\left[\, \mathbf{z}_v^{(l)} \,\|\, \mathrm{AGG}
(\{\mathbf{z}_u^{(l)} : u \in \mathcal{N}(v)\})\,\right]\right),
$$ {#eq-ch10-sage}

which supports inductive inference on unseen nodes because the aggregator is a
learned function of features rather than a lookup table
[@hamilton2017inductive]. Graph attention networks (GATs) weight neighbors with
learned attention coefficients

$$
\alpha_{vu} = \frac{\exp\!\left(\mathrm{LeakyReLU}\!\left(
\mathbf{a}^\top [\mathbf{W}\mathbf{z}_v \,\|\, \mathbf{W}\mathbf{z}_u]\right)\right)}
{\sum_{k \in \mathcal{N}(v)} \exp\!\left(\mathrm{LeakyReLU}\!\left(
\mathbf{a}^\top [\mathbf{W}\mathbf{z}_v \,\|\, \mathbf{W}\mathbf{z}_k]\right)\right)},
\qquad
\mathbf{z}_v' = \mathrm{ELU}\!\left(\sum_{u \in \mathcal{N}(v)} \alpha_{vu} \mathbf{W}\mathbf{z}_u\right),
$$ {#eq-ch10-gat}

where $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{W}$ are shared learnable parameters and $\|$
denotes vertical concatenation, allowing the model to downweight irrelevant
neighbors [@velickovic2018graph]. Graph isomorphism networks (GINs) use a sum
aggregator with an MLP and are provably as expressive as the Weisfeiler--Lehman
test for distinguishing graphs [@xu2019powerful].

| Layer | Aggregation | Inductive | Relation-aware |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| GCN [@kipf2017semi] | Degree-normalized weighted sum (@eq-ch10-gcn) | No (fixed graph) | No |
| GraphSAGE [@hamilton2017inductive] | Sampled mean / LSTM / pool (@eq-ch10-sage) | Yes | No |
| GAT [@velickovic2018graph] | Attention-weighted sum (@eq-ch10-gat) | Yes | No |
| GIN [@xu2019powerful] | Sum + MLP | Yes | No |
| R-GCN [@schlichtkrull2018modeling] | Relation-specific weighted sum (@eq-ch10-rgcn) | Yes | Yes |

The required artifact for this section is the GNN layer variants table above. The
"relation-aware" column matters for biology because most biomedical graphs are
typed: a drug *treats* a disease is not the same relation as a drug *binds* a
protein. Relational graph convolutional networks (R-GCNs) give each relation type
$r \in \mathcal{R}$ its own weight matrix $\mathbf{W}_r^{(l)}$,

$$
\mathbf{z}_v^{(l+1)} = \mathrm{ReLU}\!\left(
\sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}} \sum_{u \in \mathcal{N}_r(v)}
\frac{1}{c_{v,r}} \mathbf{W}_r^{(l)} \mathbf{z}_u^{(l)}
+ \mathbf{W}_0^{(l)} \mathbf{z}_v^{(l)} \right),
$$ {#eq-ch10-rgcn}

where $\mathcal{N}_r(v)$ is the set of neighbors of $v$ under relation $r$ and
$c_{v,r}$ is a per-node, per-relation normalization constant (typically
$|\mathcal{N}_r(v)|$) [@schlichtkrull2018modeling]. Depth introduces
over-smoothing, in which node representations converge to the same vector as
layers stack; in practice two to four layers often suffice for biological graphs.

# Knowledge-Graph Embeddings and Link Prediction

Knowledge-graph (KG) embeddings score the plausibility of triples $(h, r, t)$
rather than classifying nodes. A model $f:\mathcal{E}\times\mathcal{R}\times\mathcal{E}\to\mathbb{R}$
maps each triple to a real score, with all entity embeddings
$\{\mathbf{e}_e\}$ and relation embeddings $\{\mathbf{e}_r\}$ learned jointly.
Training treats observed triples $\mathcal{T}$ as positives and corrupted triples
as negatives, and prediction is the ranking of candidate tails for a query
$(h, r, ?)$. A common training objective maximizes

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{KG}}(\{\mathbf{e}\})
= \sum_{(h,r,t) \in \mathcal{T}}
\Big[ \log \sigma\!\left(f(h,r,t)\right)
+ \sum_{j=1}^{K} \mathbb{E}_{(h'_j, r, t'_j) \sim P_n}\!
\big( \log \sigma(-f(h'_j, r, t'_j)) \big) \Big]
$$ {#eq-ch10-kg-loss}

over all entity and relation embeddings, where each negative
$(h'_j, r, t'_j)$ is formed by corrupting the head or the tail of a true triple and
$P_n$ is the corruption distribution [@bordes2013translating]. (@eq-ch10-kg-loss) is a logistic ranking (negative-sampling) objective; its failure
mode is easy negatives, since random corruptions are often trivially false and
inflate apparent link-prediction accuracy. This is why the different score
functions below are compared only under a shared negative-sampling protocol.

TransE models a relation as a translation in the embedding space, so that the
tail is close to the head displaced by the relation vector
[@bordes2013translating]. Its score is

$$
f(h, r, t) = -\,\lVert \mathbf{e}_h + \mathbf{e}_r - \mathbf{e}_t \rVert_2,
$$ {#eq-ch10-transe}

where $\mathbf{e}_h, \mathbf{e}_r, \mathbf{e}_t \in \mathbb{R}^k$ are the
embeddings of head, relation, and tail. TransE is simple and strong on one-to-one
relations but fails on one-to-many, many-to-one, and symmetric relations. The
symmetric failure is exact: if $r$ is symmetric then both $(h,r,t)$ and $(t,r,h)$
are true, and requiring a high score (@eq-ch10-transe) for both forces

$$
\mathbf{e}_h + \mathbf{e}_r \approx \mathbf{e}_t
\quad \text{and} \quad
\mathbf{e}_t + \mathbf{e}_r \approx \mathbf{e}_h
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
2\,\mathbf{e}_r \approx \mathbf{0}
\;\;\text{and}\;\;
\mathbf{e}_h \approx \mathbf{e}_t,
$$ {#eq-ch10-transe-sym}

(@eq-ch10-transe-sym) drives the relation vector to the origin and collapses
every entity participating in a symmetric relation to the same point, destroying
their distinguishability; the same argument makes one-to-many relations
non-identifiable, since $(h,r,t_1)$ and $(h,r,t_2)$ force
$\mathbf{e}_{t_1} \approx \mathbf{e}_{t_2}$ [@bordes2013translating]. This
non-identifiability is the motivation for rotation- and product-based scores.

RotatE models each relation as a rotation in complex space, so a relation can map
one head to several tails. Writing the complex embeddings
$\mathbf{e}_h, \mathbf{e}_t \in \mathbb{C}^k$ with per-coordinate modulus at most
one, the score is

$$
f(h, r, t) = -\,\lVert \mathbf{e}_h \odot \mathbf{e}_r - \mathbf{e}_t \rVert_2,
\qquad
e_r[j] = e^{\,i\theta_j},
$$ {#eq-ch10-rotate}

where $\odot$ is the Hadamard product and $\theta_j$ is the phase of relation $r$
in dimension $j$; the constraint $|e_r[j]| = 1$ makes $\mathbf{e}_r$ a unit-modulus
rotation [@sun2019rotate]. Because rotations compose, RotatE represents symmetry
($\theta_j \in \{0, \pi\}$), antisymmetry ($\theta_j \notin \{0,\pi\}$ gives
$\mathbf{e}_r \neq \mathbf{e}_r^{-1}$), inversion, and composition patterns that
TransE cannot; its limitations are the fixed dimensional budget and the fact that
composition in its relation space is additive in the phases $\theta_j$ and hence
commutative, so it cannot represent a non-commutative composition pattern.

DistMult simplifies the bilinear family to a real trilinear score,

$$
f(h, r, t) = \sum_{j} e_h[j]\, e_r[j]\, e_t[j],
$$ {#eq-ch10-distmult}

which is efficient but manifestly symmetric in head and tail,
$f(h,r,t) = f(t,r,h)$, and therefore cannot represent directed or antisymmetric
relations: for any antisymmetric relation the model must assign the same score to
$(h,r,t)$ and $(t,r,h)$, so it cannot rank one above the other
[@yang2015embedding].

ComplEx restores asymmetry with a complex bilinear product. For
$\mathbf{e}_h, \mathbf{e}_r, \mathbf{e}_t \in \mathbb{C}^k$, the score is

$$
f(h, r, t) = \mathrm{Re}\!\left(\langle \mathbf{e}_h, \mathbf{e}_r, \overline{\mathbf{e}_t} \rangle\right)
= \mathrm{Re}\!\left(\sum_{j} e_h[j]\, e_r[j]\, \overline{e_t[j]}\right),
$$ {#eq-ch10-complex}

where the bar denotes complex conjugation [@trouillon2016complex]. ComplEx models
antisymmetry: writing $\Re(e_\ast[j]) = a_\ast^{(j)}$ and
$\Im(e_\ast[j]) = b_\ast^{(j)}$, the difference between a triple and its reversal
is

$$
f(h,r,t) - f(t,r,h)
= 2 \sum_{j} b_r^{(j)}
\!\left( a_h^{(j)} b_t^{(j)} - a_t^{(j)} b_h^{(j)} \right),
$$ {#eq-ch10-complex-antisym}

(@eq-ch10-complex-antisym) is nonzero whenever some relation coordinate has
nonzero imaginary part $b_r^{(j)} \neq 0$ and the head and tail embeddings are not
trivially aligned; the score is therefore genuinely asymmetric, unlike DistMult (the real special case
$\Im \equiv 0$) [@trouillon2016complex]. Note that a high score for $(h,r,t)$ no
longer implies a high score for $(t,r,h)$, which is exactly what directed
biomedical relations such as *treats* or *binds* require. The choice among these
models therefore follows the relational patterns present in the graph, summarized
by which of symmetry, antisymmetry, inversion, and composition each can represent.

::: {#fig-kg-linkpred}
**Figure description.** Knowledge-graph link prediction. A heterogeneous graph
contains typed entities (drug $d$, protein $p$, disease $s$) connected by typed
relations (binds, associated with, treats). The model embeds every entity and
relation and scores each candidate triple by a relation-specific function $f(h, r,
t)$ — translation for TransE (@eq-ch10-transe), rotation for RotatE (@eq-ch10-rotate), or a
bilinear product for DistMult (@eq-ch10-distmult) and ComplEx (@eq-ch10-complex). For a query
$(d, \text{treats}, ?)$, the model ranks all diseases by their scores; the
highest-ranked true-but-unobserved disease is the link-prediction output,
evaluated by mean reciprocal rank and Hits@$K$.
:::

A descriptive figure of the link-prediction workflow is given in
@fig-kg-linkpred. The evaluation protocol — corrupt the tail (and head), score
positives against negatives, and report mean reciprocal rank and Hits@$K$ — is
shared across TransE, RotatE, ComplEx, and DistMult, which makes their results
comparable when the same negative-sampling scheme is used. See Chapter 11 for the
pitfalls of biased or easy negative sampling.

# Applications

The three prediction tasks now separate cleanly. *Node classification* predicts a
property of a node, such as the functional class of a protein. *Link prediction*
predicts whether an edge exists or will exist, such as a novel drug--target
interaction. *Knowledge-graph completion* predicts the missing tail of a typed
triple, such as the disease a drug may treat.

Drug repurposing is the most prominent KG application. Hetionet integrates
heterogeneous biomedical knowledge into a single graph and shows that a graph
algorithm connecting compounds to diseases can prioritize existing drugs for new
indications [@himmelstein2017systematic]. Decagon extends this idea to
polypharmacy by modeling drug--drug side effects and the underlying
protein--protein interactions with a relational GCN (@eq-ch10-rgcn), treating
side-effect prediction as a link-prediction problem over typed edges
[@zitnik2018modeling].

Target identification reuses the same machinery in the opposite direction: given
a disease, rank proteins or genes by their connection to disease-associated nodes.
Function prediction applies GNNs to protein structure graphs; DeepFRI, for
example, trains a graph convolutional network (@eq-ch10-gcn) on residue contact graphs
to predict Gene Ontology terms, showing that structure-derived graph embeddings
transfer to function annotation [@gligorijevic2021structure]. In each case the
embedding is not the end product — the ranking of candidate edges or labels is.

Node classification on interaction graphs is the natural counterpart of link
prediction. The setting is inductive when the model must annotate nodes that were
absent during training, which occurs whenever a new screen adds proteins to an
existing network. GraphSAGE (@eq-ch10-sage) evaluates exactly this regime on
protein--protein interaction graphs, predicting functional roles from a node's own
features and an aggregate of its neighbors' features rather than from a fixed
lookup table [@hamilton2017inductive]. The same inductive property is what allows
a GNN trained on one organism's network to embed a related organism's nodes
without retraining, provided that node features are defined consistently across
the two graphs.

A recurring methodological point links these applications. The graph is almost
always incomplete, so a model that scores only observed edges learns to reproduce
the biases of the databases on which it was trained. Reporting link-prediction
quality therefore requires held-out edges sampled in a way that respects the
graph's structure, and it requires distinguishing performance on edges that are
easy to guess from high-degree hubs from performance on the sparse periphery. The
evaluation protocols of Chapter 11 apply directly here; the graph-specific
complication is that random edge splits leak information through shared
neighborhoods far more readily than random splits of independent examples.

# Heterogeneity and Scale

Two practical pressures dominate. The first is heterogeneity: biomedical graphs
contain several node and edge types, and a homogeneous GNN must collapse them,
losing relational information. Relational GCNs (@eq-ch10-rgcn) address typed edges
[@schlichtkrull2018modeling], and metapath2vec generalizes random-walk embeddings
to heterogeneous networks by guiding walks along typed meta-paths — for example
drug→protein→disease — so that co-occurrence statistics respect relation
types [@dong2017metapath2vec]. The second pressure is scale: biomedical knowledge
graphs reach millions of nodes and tens of millions of edges, which makes
full-batch training and dense attention infeasible. Sampling-based training, as in
GraphSAGE, and standardized large-scale benchmarks such as the Open Graph
Benchmark make results reproducible and comparable [@hu2020open]. Temporal and
multiplex graphs add a further axis: edges appear and vanish over time and the
same node participates in several edge types, so a single static embedding is an
approximation that must be justified by the task.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key Takeaways
- Node, edge, and knowledge-graph prediction are distinct tasks; the embedding
  and the evaluation metric must match the task.
- Shallow embeddings (DeepWalk, node2vec, LINE) factorize co-occurrence over
  walks (@eq-ch10-walk-sgns) and are strong on homogeneous graphs but cannot embed
  unseen nodes.
- GNNs generalize these methods through permutation-invariant message passing
  (@eq-ch10-mp); GCN (@eq-ch10-gcn), GraphSAGE (@eq-ch10-sage), GAT (@eq-ch10-gat), GIN, and R-GCN
  (@eq-ch10-rgcn) differ in aggregation and in whether they handle relation types.
- KG embeddings score typed triples; TransE (@eq-ch10-transe), RotatE (@eq-ch10-rotate),
  DistMult (@eq-ch10-distmult), and ComplEx (@eq-ch10-complex) encode different relational
  patterns, so the model must match the graph's relations.
- Biomedical graphs are heterogeneous, sparse, and heavy-tailed, so relation-aware
  and sampling-based models are usually necessary at scale.
:::

## Further Reading

- Perozzi, Al-Rfou, and Skiena, *DeepWalk* (2014) [@perozzi2014deepwalk] — the
  origin of random-walk node embeddings.
- Grover and Leskovec, *node2vec* (2016) [@grover2016node2vec] — biased walks and
  the community-versus-role trade-off.
- Kipf and Welling, *Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional
  Networks* (2017) [@kipf2017semi] — the canonical GCN layer.
- Hamilton, Ying, and Leskovec, *Inductive Representation Learning on Large
  Graphs* (2017) [@hamilton2017inductive] — GraphSAGE and inductive inference.
- Veličković et al., *Graph Attention Networks* (2018) [@velickovic2018graph] —
  attention over neighbors.
- Bordes et al., *Translating Embeddings for Modeling Multi-relational Data*
  (2013) [@bordes2013translating] and Sun et al., *RotatE* (2019)
  [@sun2019rotate] — the reference points for knowledge-graph completion.
